messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 51
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Widowed
- Occupation: School Principal
- Trauma Type: Life-threatening illness
- Pcl5: 56

At fifty-one, he is a school principal who is used to being the one who steadies other people. Teachers come into his office frustrated or overwhelmed, parents arrive angry, students cry or refuse to speak, and he has built a life around staying measured and useful. When he talks about what happened to him, though, that steadiness seems borrowed. He tells the story carefully, as if too much feeling at once might knock something loose.

Three years ago, in late autumn, he is still recently widowed and trying to hold his life together through routine. His wife has been gone less than a year. He gets up before dawn, answers emails over coffee, drives to school while listening to the local news, and stays late to avoid going home to a house that feels abruptly too large. He tells himself work is keeping him afloat. Then he starts feeling run down in a way that does not fit grief alone. At first he blames the long hours: a strange heaviness in his limbs, shortness of breath when he climbs the stairs, nights of sweating through his T-shirt. He ignores it for weeks, then months. He prides himself on being dependable and dislikes making a fuss.

What finally sends him to the hospital is a morning assembly. He is speaking to a gym full of middle school students when his vision narrows and the room begins to tilt. He remembers gripping the podium and seeing one of the teachers stand up suddenly in the front row. After that, the story comes back in flashes: fluorescent lights rushing overhead, clipped voices, someone cutting off his shirt, the metallic smell of blood, a doctor saying they need to move quickly. He had a severe, life-threatening illness that escalates fast, faster than he can make sense of it. In his memory, the central fact is not medical but existential: one ordinary workday becomes a day when he is no longer sure he will live through the night.

He spends weeks in the hospital. He says the worst part is the helplessness. Since his wife’s death he has been surviving by managing details, but in the hospital there is no managing, only waiting. Machines beep relentlessly. Staff enter at all hours. He startles awake disoriented, unsure whether it is morning or midnight. He becomes preoccupied with every sensation in his body. A spike in pain, a skipped heartbeat, a cough—each one feels like the beginning of the end. Sometimes he lies still and imagines who will clean out his office, who will tell the students, whether anyone will remember to water the plants in his kitchen window. Because he is already a widower, the possibility of dying carries a particular loneliness. He tells no one this at the time, but some nights he is more frightened by the image of dying alone than by the illness itself.

He survives, and people around him use words like lucky, miraculous, resilient. He says thank you and returns to work before he feels ready. From the outside, he looks almost the same. He wears a tie, walks the halls, stands at basketball games, jokes with the custodian. Inside, his world has narrowed. He cannot stop scanning for signs that his body is failing again. If a teacher mentions someone’s cancer diagnosis, his stomach drops. If the school nurse pages him unexpectedly, he feels a burst of adrenaline so intense he has to grip his desk. Medical dramas on television are impossible now. Even the antiseptic smell of the nurse’s office can send him back to the hospital so vividly that for a moment he feels the bed rails under his hands.

Nights are the hardest. He sleeps lightly, waking at 2:00 or 3:00 a.m. with his heart pounding, certain something is terribly wrong. He checks his pulse, sits on the edge of the bed, argues with himself about whether to call 911. Sometimes he walks from room to room in the dark house, unable to settle. The silence there feels different since the illness. After his wife died, it felt empty; now it also feels unsafe. He keeps a lamp on in the hallway because waking in darkness reminds him of the hospital room before dawn, when he would open his eyes and not immediately know if he had made it through the night.

At school, he notices changes in himself that trouble him. He is more irritable with staff, less patient with students who complain of minor ailments. Then he feels ashamed, because part of him knows they are only children. He avoids taking the stairs where he nearly collapsed. He reschedules his own follow-up appointments twice, then berates himself for it. He tells colleagues he is “fine” because he cannot bear the look that comes over people’s faces when they hear how sick he was. On bad days, he closes his office door and sits very still, waiting for a wave of panic to pass while the intercom crackles outside.

He says the illness taught him that life can change in an instant, but he does not say it with gratitude. He says it with vigilance. Even now, years later, he lives as if catastrophe is not a possibility but an expectation. He continues to show up for his school, remembering birthdays, mediating conflicts, praising students at assemblies. Yet beneath that practiced calm, he is braced. His body no longer feels like a place he can trust, and the ordinary school day he once relied on now seems threaded with danger he cannot quite name but never fully stops anticipating.
